local_articles.title: Literacy coach boosts Portage kids’ reading scores
local_articles.summary: Literacy coach boosts Portage kids’ reading scores  Chicago Tribune
local_articles.full_content:
Reading scores at Central Elementary School in Portage have increased dramatically since a literacy coach began working with teachers.

Central is among the schools required by state law, beginning in 2022-2023, to have an instructional coach because of IREAD-3 pass rates below 70%.

The Indiana Literacy Cadre’s goal is to have 95% of students taking the IREAD-3 test pass by 2027.

The idea is to make sure students are able to read by the time they finish third grade, so they have a solid foundation for continued learning.

IREAD-3 is now administered statewide in second grade.

“We love the idea of literacy coaches, but as you know, funding is something that we really have to keep an eye on,” Director of Grants and Assessments Linda Williams said.

The goal is to eventually have one coach for every two elementary schools, Superintendent Amanda Alaniz said.

“It’s really important that you see the growth rate that Central Elem experienced,” Williams said.

In 2024, 66.1% of Central students taking the IREAD-3 passed the test, well below the threshold. But just a year later, 86.8% passed, literacy coach Tabitha Henry told the Portage Township School Board on Monday, for a jump of 20.7 percentage points, the highest in the school district.

Not counting all the students eligible for a good cause exemption, and 100% of Central’s remaining students passed. That compares to a statewide average of 92.5%.

Under the state guidelines, Henry is required to be in the classroom one to three times a week. “I actually go in the classroom four times a week, and I teach with them,” she said.

“I really admire going in four to five times a week,” board Vice President Wilma Vazquez said.

“Teachers can attend professional development teaching sessions,” but hands-on help in the classroom is better than just telling teachers what to do, she said. The teachers and the students aren’t the only ones who benefit.

“We have some wonderful teachers at Central, and I’ve learned a lot from them,” Henry said. She meets with her colleagues and mentors elsewhere, too, for additional training.

“Obviously, what you’re doing is working. Those are dramatic results,” board President Andy Maletta said.

“The changes that you see, it helps to have support at the ground level for our teachers,” Alaniz said.

“On-demand learning for our educators is going to be the best way for them to hit the ground running,” she added.

Students are given before and after assessments – the identical test – to measure their progress. In one class, the number exceeding the goal rose from 14% beforehand to 83% afterward. The number struggling the worst fell from 63% beforehand to 11% afterward, Henry’s data showed.

Maletta asked, “Can we clone you?”

Next year, Henry will stay at Central and add Myers Elementary to her portfolio, Alaniz said.

With one literacy coach per two elementaries, the coaches will focus on kindergarten through second grade with some help for third grade, too. “We think that can be managed,” Alaniz said.

In other business, the board approved a $2.6 million contract for a roof for the new Aylesworth Middle School, which will replace Willowcreek Middle School, and a $25,840 contract with Alliance Environmental Solutions for asbestos abatement at the former IT building just west of Aylesworth Elementary School.

Work on the new middle school project will begin in just a few weeks.

In about four weeks, crews will start digging a detention pond. In June, the former IT building will be razed, with demolition of the former Aylesworth Elementary to begin around July 15.

Deliveries to the construction site will be scheduled to avoid the times when students are arriving or leaving, project manager Paul Todoroski said.

Doug Ross is a freelance reporter for the Post-Tribune.

local_articles.title: Literacy retention bill passes Missouri Senate committee
local_articles.summary: Literacy retention bill passes Missouri Senate committee  Jefferson City News Tribune
local_articles.full_content:
# Literacy retention bill passes Missouri Senate committee



April 29, 2026



by






[Jack Wardynski](https://www.californiademocrat.com/staff/jack-wardynski)

×![The Missouri State Capitol in Jefferson City, as pictured September 26, 2023 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).](https://faughnmedia.media.clients.ellingtoncms.com/imports/adg/img/2025/08/22/210871120_092623_mocapitol1-1536x1021_t320.jpg?fa67021387348b8667950d2a49bd5d6642c5ab68)

An education bill in the Missouri Senate would raise literacy standards for elementary students.

House Bill 2872 would create the Missouri Reading Screener, an assessment that grades a student's reading proficiency. Third-grade students identified as "at-risk" by the assessment would be automatically retained in their grade level.

The bill, sponsored by Cathy Jo Loy, R-Carthage, earned bipartisan approval in the House with a 131-10 vote and passed through the Senate Education Committee on Tuesday morning.

"Reading success is not about talent, it's about instruction," Loy said during a Jan. 28 hearing of the House Elementary and Secondary Education Committee. "We are not trying to retain children. We are trying to make retention unnecessary by fixing literacy early."

According to Loy, the bill identifies four key areas of reading instruction for Missouri students. The first is removing the three-cueing system from schools. This system uses structure, meaning and sound cues to help children determine the meaning of words. Missouri would join around a dozen other states in banning the method that has been criticized by reading specialists.

The bill would also re-establish phonics as the foundation of reading, bolster early identification and help for struggling students, and strengthen interventions for dyslexia instruction, Joy said.

Students from grades 1-3 would be required to take the assessment three times per year, starting in the 2027-28 school year. The assessment would grade them from "at-risk" to "exceeds expectations." For "at-risk" second-grade students, parents or guardians must meet with their teacher to create an intervention plan for additional instruction.

At the same time, the bill allows for good-cause exemptions to be granted to students in special circumstances. These could include students with a learning disability who require an individualized education plan or children with less than two years of English language instruction.

Beyond the reading assessment, the bill promises to structurally improve literacy instruction statewide. Beginning in 2027, DESE would be required to provide annual assessments of educator preparation programs to determine if they are sufficient for evidence-based reading instruction. It would also expand capabilities of reading tutoring programs.

"Retention is the tourniquet. The cure is fixing reading instruction," Loy said.

Despite widespread support from state legislators, some local educators and school administrators have pushed back on HB 2872.

"There are very few instructional strategies that lead to negative student achievement gains. Retention is one," California Superintendent Daniel Williams said. "Retaining kids does not help them learn better because of the offset of all the psychological trauma and embarrassment with that."

Williams said he feels it is premature to implement a bill like this, as reading scores for students statewide are increasing.

Cole R-5 Superintendent Charley Burch shares many of Williams' thoughts on the bill.

"I certainly understand and appreciate the legislature's intent. Strengthening early literacy and ensuring students are supported for long term success is a goal I think everyone shares," he wrote in an email to the News Tribune. "That said, I do have some reservations about the automatic retention component of the bill. I strongly believe in local control and in the professional judgment of our educators ... Mandating retention based solely on assessment outcomes removes important flexibility and does not allow for the full picture of a student's development to be considered."

Burch also pointed out the "significant literary reform" introduced by the state via the Language Essentials for Teachers of Reading and Spelling training (LETRS). DESE implemented the program during the 2023-24 school year to help strengthen literacy instruction across Missouri. Burch wrote "we simply do not yet have enough data" to accurately measure the impact of the new training, and implementing new legislature related to elementary retention is not "prudent."

"As a state, we've always prided ourselves on local control, right? And now the state is gonna tell us, 'We're gonna create an assessment that will determine whether you are forced to retain every one of these third-graders.' So that is not equitable," Williams said. "It makes zero sense."

HB 2872 earned a 4-1 vote of approval during executive session Tuesday, with Sen. Maggie Nurrenbern, D-Clay County, as the lone dissenter. The bill now advances to the Senate floor.

\-\-\----

[House Bill 2872](https://house.mo.gov/Bill.aspx?bill=HB2872&year=2026&code=R): Creates, repeals and modifies provisions relating to literacy of elementary school students.

Sponsor: Rep. Cathy Jo Loy, R-Carthage.

# Opinion: How Gen Z’s energy literacy crisis is costing Alaska

By Drake Ward

Published: 1 day ago

![](https://www.adn.com/resizer/v2/KLXVMKX2J2WZ2JVMYCKM6HA2ZE.jpg?auth=1e8a6d36a2a83d04e53ad224c46e529c24523f37ae734bfcc72390612855662d&width=800&height=533)A Gen Z young woman use her phone to produce a TikTok video. (AP Photo/Bebeto Matthews)

Growing up in Anchorage, I never had to think twice about where energy came from. The people around me worked to provide it — winters on the Slope, on the pipeline, in the support industries that keep extraction running. Energy was never abstract; it was someone’s job, someone’s livelihood, the backbone of the state’s economy that guided the everyday lives of thousands.

Then I left for university out of state, and I started hearing things that genuinely stopped me midconversation.

A professor described drilling in the Arctic as destructive and “uniquely evil.” A university administrator, when I mentioned I wanted to work in Alaska resource development law, immediately began preaching about the dangers of resource development, assuming I wanted Alaska to remain a snow globe for the rest of the country to look upon and smile at: beautiful, fragile and untouched.

This is the energy literacy crisis of my generation. It is costing real people real things.

My peers and I are the most energy-consuming generation in history. We stream constantly, charge devices that never leave our hands and have transitioned to a more online world. Yet we also register [the highest opposition](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2021/05/PS_2021.05.26_climate-and-generations_REPORT.pdf "https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2021/05/PS_2021.05.26_climate-and-generations_REPORT.pdf") to offshore oil and gas drilling of any demographic group in modern polling. This isn’t hypocritical; it’s what happens when a generation grows up never asking where power comes from.

When my classmates plug in their laptops, they aren’t questioning what made that simple action possible. They aren’t thinking about the natural gas plant that generated the electricity, or about the pipeline that delivered the fuel, or about the federal permitting process that took years to approve. To them, electricity comes from the wall. The physical infrastructure that converts raw resources into usable energy is invisible to the people consuming it most, and in a democracy, the people who don’t think about how something works still get to vote on whether it continues.

Alaska is where that abstraction has the sharpest consequences. Oil and gas revenues have made up considerable portions of Alaska’s budget for decades. The men and women I grew up around worked long days in difficult conditions in one of the harshest environments on Earth. When someone who has never been to Alaska decides it should be preserved like a decorative object on the mantle, they are making a fiscal and economic argument on behalf of people they have never met, with consequences they will never experience.

ADVERTISEMENT

What makes this harder is that the clean energy transition doesn’t escape this logic; a renewable future requires an enormous expansion of resource extraction. Wind turbines, battery storage and grid upgrades need lithium, cobalt and copper. The discussion is more about where, under what rules and whether the people whose lives depend on those decisions have any voice in them.

I want to be a natural resources attorney in Alaska. I came to that goal because I grew up understanding, in a way most of my university classmates do not, that the lights stay on because someone is doing hard, consequential work to make it happen. I think that work should be regulated. I think environmental concerns are legitimate. I also think that informed opposition is categorically different from reflexive opposition, and right now, most of what shapes energy policy toward Alaska is the latter.

Before my generation votes on, litigates against or protests the industries powering our lives, we owe it to the people on the other end of those decisions to understand what we’re actually talking about. Snow globes may be decorative, but the people inside them most certainly are not.

_**Drake Ward**_ _is a freshman as Saint Louis University studying history, political science, philosophy and economics. From Anchorage, he is a former intern for Sen. Lisa Murkowski and an incoming intern at the National Security Institute._

# Penn State launches AI literacy course for employees

Georgianna Sutherland / For Spotlight PA


# Penn State launches AI literacy course for employees

Students will have access to training this fall

![Pittsburgh Post-Gazette logo](https://www.post-gazette.com/assets-1y/images/misc/pg-logo-100px-green-byline.png)

Maddie Aiken

Pittsburgh Post-Gazette

[maiken@post-gazette.com](mailto:maiken@post-gazette.com)

Apr 28, 2026

6:01 PM

Penn State has launched an artificial intelligence literacy course for faculty and staff as part of its efforts to be one step ahead of AI’s sweep through higher education.

Students will soon likewise have access to the training, which aims to equip participants with the knowledge, skills and “ethical grounding” necessary to engage with AI in academic and professional settings.

The course is one example of Penn State’s commitment to “responsible, human-centered AI knowledge and use,” Provost Fotis Sotiropoulos said during Tuesday’s faculty senate meeting.

Advertisement

“As I've said on a number of occasions, AI is not about tools and chatbots. It's about unleashing human potential and creativity using these powerful tools, and that's what we strive to do here across the community,” Mr. Sotiropoulos said.

[![A University of Pittsburgh student rides an e-scooter along Fifth Ave. in Oakland on Tuesday, March 24, 2026.](https://73f3e7d5672db1849e6c-6434aaf008a29447cc424990bc6a54a7.ssl.cf2.rackcdn.com/stories/202603250073/300x_a1-1_cTC/20260325jgescooter1_1774633690.jpg)\\
\\
Maddie Aiken\\
\\
After Penn State’s crackdown on e-scooters, Pitt students want similar regulations](https://www.post-gazette.com/news/education/2026/03/28/electric-scooter-college-students/stories/202603250073)

“...Whoever says that universities take long to change, I'm enormously proud by how fast this community moved to really bring forward all of this innovation in AI — human-centered AI.”

Titled “AI Essentials,” the course consists of four modules that will teach participants the following:

- What AI is, how it works, and how to recognize, question and use it
- How to evaluate AI outputs and decide when using AI makes sense
- What AI tools are available at Penn State and how to use them

Faculty and staff currently have access to the training. Penn State leaders expect faculty to incorporate the training in their classes and curricula, Mr. Sotiropoulos said.

Advertisement

The course will launch for most students this fall. A small cohort of students enrolled in summer courses will have early access to a pilot program in the upcoming weeks.

Penn State’s goal is for all of its students to be “AI literate” by the end of their freshman year, Mr. Sotiropoulos said. He urged faculty to encourage students to complete the training. Freshmen will also receive a preview of it during new student orientation.

“This is a commitment that we have made to our community, and we're working really hard to make it happen,” the provost said.

Earlier this semester, the university announced that “AI literacy” would be one of several broad initiatives as it prioritizes AI-forward thinking.

[![Penn State Fayette, near Uniontown on Wednesday, May 21, 2025.  ](https://73f3e7d5672db1849e6c-6434aaf008a29447cc424990bc6a54a7.ssl.cf2.rackcdn.com/stories/202604010091/300x_a1-1_cTC/20250521SFPennStateClosureh2-001-12_1775072846.jpg)\\
\\
Maddie Aiken\\
\\
Penn State preparations for branch campus closures in full swing](https://www.post-gazette.com/news/education/2026/04/01/penn-state-preparations-commonwealth-campus-closures/stories/202604010091)

Other initiatives [include](https://www.psu.edu/news/administration/story/penn-state-makes-strategic-investments-prepare-students-ai-driven-future):

- Creating a new administrative role, vice provost for AI, who will be tasked with shaping and advancing the university’s AI strategy
- Recruiting dozens of new faculty members with expertise in foundational AI, data science, material science, rural health, human-centered computing, education, creative arts and applied AI fields
- Introducing a secure enterprise AI platform, which will be available to all students, faculty and staff


First Published: April 28, 2026, 6:01 p.m.
